items: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
Sea otters wrap themselves in kelp so they don't drift away while they sleep.
Flamingos get their pink color from the food they eat.
A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute.
Giraffes have seven bones in their necks, the same number as people.
Some Asian elephants can recognize themselves in a mirror.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
Emperor penguin dads keep the egg warm on their feet for about two months.
A sea star can grow back a lost arm.
Honeybees do a waggle dance to tell each other where to find flowers.
An owl can turn its head about 270 degrees.
Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, sprinting at about 60 miles an hour.
Sloths move so slowly that algae can grow in their fur.
The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
Male seahorses carry the eggs in a pouch until the babies hatch.
Crows can remember the faces of individual people for years.
Each bottlenose dolphin has its own signature whistle that works like a name.
No two zebras have exactly the same stripes.
Under their thick white fur, polar bears have black skin.
An axolotl can regrow a lost leg, and even parts of its heart.
A woodpecker's long tongue wraps around the back of its skull.
A chameleon's tongue can be longer than its body.
Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year.
Monarch butterflies can fly up to 3,000 miles to spend the winter in Mexico.
Most frogs don't drink with their mouths and soak up water through their skin.
Horses can doze standing up thanks to a locking system in their legs.
A rabbit's teeth never stop growing.
A pangolin's scales are made of keratin, like your fingernails.
Ostriches lay the largest eggs of any living bird.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
Fireflies make light with a chemical reaction that gives off almost no heat.
Male humpback whales sing long songs that can go on for hours.
Giant pandas spend about 10 to 16 hours a day eating bamboo.
A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
Sharks have been around for longer than trees.
A tardigrade can survive being frozen, dried out, and even sent into space.
A kiwi bird's egg can weigh up to about a fifth as much as its mother.
Snakes smell by flicking out their tongues to pick up scents.
Hippos ooze a reddish fluid from their skin that works like a natural sunscreen.
A beaver's front teeth have iron in their enamel, which helps make them tough.
Gorillas build fresh nests to sleep in every night.
Some spiders travel on the wind by riding silk threads, called ballooning.
Hermit crabs move into bigger shells as they grow.
Dragonflies can fly forward, backward, and hover in place.
Puffins can hold a dozen or more small fish in their beaks at once.
Red pandas use their bushy tails as blankets in the cold.
Capybaras are the largest rodents in the world.
Woolly mammoths still lived on an Arctic island when the pyramids were built.
A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
Jupiter spins so fast that a day there lasts only about 10 hours.
Saturn is so light for its size that it is less dense than water.
Uranus spins on its side, tipped over at about 98 degrees.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the solar system.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
More than a million Earths could fit inside the Sun.
The Moon drifts about 1.5 inches farther from Earth every year.
Footprints left on the Moon could last for millions of years.
Nights on Mercury drop to about minus 290 degrees Fahrenheit.
One year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.
Pluto has a giant heart-shaped plain of ice called Tombaugh Regio.
Astronauts grow a little taller in space as their spines stretch out.
Halley's Comet swings back past Earth about every 76 years.
A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh about a billion tons.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has raged for more than 150 years.
Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice.
The first animals sent into space were fruit flies, in 1947.
There are more trees on Earth than stars in our galaxy.
The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away.
The Moon has quakes of its own, called moonquakes.
Each Voyager probe carries a golden record of sounds and music from Earth.
Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light on its way to us.
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes and seas of liquid methane.
Scientists think Jupiter's moon Europa has a salty ocean under its ice.
Saturn's moon Enceladus shoots jets of icy water out into space.
A light-year is a distance, about 6 trillion miles.
Proxima Centauri, the closest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light-years away.
A comet's tail always points away from the Sun.
The rocks in the asteroid belt are so spread out that spacecraft fly right through.
The center of the Sun is about 27 million degrees Fahrenheit.
Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Neptune was found with math before anyone saw it through a telescope.
Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.
The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, can be seen without a telescope.
An astronaut hit golf balls on the Moon in 1971.
Our solar system takes about 230 million years to circle the Milky Way.
Earth's air glows with auroras when particles from the Sun hit it.
Babies start with nearly 300 bones, and many fuse to make an adult's 206.
The smallest bone in your body is the stirrup bone in your middle ear.
The thighbone is the longest bone in the human body.
At about 70 beats a minute, your heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Your brain uses about 20 percent of your body's energy.
An adult human body is made of roughly 30 trillion cells.
Hiccups happen when your diaphragm suddenly tightens.
Goose bumps happen when tiny muscles pull your hairs upright.
Your left lung is a bit smaller than your right, to make room for your heart.
Your small intestine is about 20 feet long.
The clear front of your eye, the cornea, has no blood vessels.
You can't tickle yourself because your brain knows the touch is coming.
Skin is the largest organ of the human body.
Kids have 20 baby teeth, and adults have up to 32 permanent ones.
Your heart has its own natural pacemaker that keeps it beating.
A red blood cell lives for about 120 days.
Hair on your head grows about half an inch a month.
Yawning is contagious, and even reading about yawns can start one.
About 60 percent of an adult's body is water.
The brain itself can't feel pain.
You are a little taller in the morning than at bedtime.
Taste buds are replaced about every week or two.
The picture at the back of your eye is upside down, and your brain flips it.
Your fingers have no muscles inside them and are moved by tendons.
Kneecaps start out as soft cartilage and harden into bone years later.
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface.
The deepest spot in the ocean, the Challenger Deep, is nearly 7 miles down.
Set Mount Everest in the deepest ocean trench and its peak would still be underwater.
Tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton make about half the oxygen on Earth.
The ocean is salty because rivers carry minerals from rocks into the sea.
The Great Barrier Reef stretches about 1,400 miles along Australia.
Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps.
Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
The Atlantic Ocean grows about an inch wider every year.
Ocean tides are caused mostly by the Moon's pull.
The Bay of Fundy in Canada has some of the highest tides on Earth.
Anglerfish use a glowing lure on their heads to find food in the dark deep sea.
Giant squid have eyes about as big as dinner plates.
Giant kelp can grow about 2 feet in a single day.
Jellyfish have no brain, no heart, and no bones.
Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
The Gulf Stream carries warm water up the US East Coast and across the Atlantic.
About 90 percent of an iceberg is hidden underwater.
Seawater freezes at about 28 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than fresh water.
The longest mountain range on Earth runs mostly under the sea.
Clownfish all hatch as males, and some later become females.
A narwhal's long tusk is actually a tooth.
Deep-sea vents host whole communities of life that never see sunlight.
The largest waterfall on Earth is underwater, in the Denmark Strait.
Point Nemo is the spot in the ocean farthest from any land.
Manatees are sometimes called sea cows and are related to elephants.
Krill are tiny shrimp-like animals, and blue whales eat tons of them a day.
No sunlight reaches deeper than about 3,300 feet below the ocean's surface.
Seals and sea lions are related, but only sea lions have little ear flaps.
Sea sponges are animals, even though they look like plants.
Some kinds of bamboo can grow about 3 feet in a single day.
Botanically speaking, bananas are berries but strawberries are not.
Young sunflowers turn to follow the Sun across the sky.
Giant sequoias are the largest trees on Earth by volume.
The tallest trees on Earth are coast redwoods, some over 350 feet tall.
Some bristlecone pines in California are more than 4,000 years old.
A Venus flytrap snaps shut when a bug touches its trigger hairs twice.
Peanuts are not nuts at all but legumes, like peas and beans.
Cactus spines are a kind of leaf.
The largest single flower in the world can be about 3 feet wide.
A date palm seed about 2,000 years old was sprouted into a living tree.
It takes about 40 gallons of maple sap to make one gallon of syrup.
Dandelion seeds ride the wind on tiny parachutes.
The coco de mer palm makes the largest seed of any plant.
Leaves change color in fall when their green chlorophyll fades away.
Early carrots were purple or yellow, not orange.
Vanilla comes from the seed pods of an orchid.
Cinnamon is the dried inner bark of a tree.
The sensitive plant folds up its leaves when you touch them.
A baobab tree can store thousands of gallons of water in its trunk.
Coffee beans are the seeds of a small red fruit.
Pando, a grove of aspens in Utah, is a single living thing joined by one root system.
Lotus leaves stay clean because water beads up and rolls the dirt away.
Ginkgo trees are called living fossils because their family is so ancient.
Some plants, like the pitcher plant, trap insects for food.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The first Olympic Games were held in ancient Greece about 2,800 years ago.
The Pantheon in Rome has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
The oldest surviving camera photograph was made in France around 1827.
The Wright brothers' first airplane flight in 1903 lasted 12 seconds.
The first hot air balloon passengers were a sheep, a duck, and a rooster.
The Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for only 20 years.
The Statue of Liberty turned green as its copper skin weathered.
Ancient Egyptians played a board game called senet.
Chess grew out of a game played in India about 1,500 years ago.
Johannes Gutenberg built his printing press with movable type around 1440.
Before rubber erasers, people rubbed out pencil marks with bread.
Norse explorers reached North America about 500 years before Columbus.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa started to lean while it was still being built.
China was the first place to use paper money, about 1,000 years ago.
The world's first postage stamp, the Penny Black, came out in Britain in 1840.
Stonehenge was built in stages, starting about 5,000 years ago.
The first crossword puzzle ran in a New York newspaper in 1913.
The teddy bear was named after President Theodore Roosevelt.
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod.
The Great Wall of China, with all its branches, is over 13,000 miles long.
Flutes carved from bird bone over 40,000 years ago are among the oldest instruments.
The cave paintings at Lascaux in France are about 17,000 years old.
Dogs were the first animals people tamed, at least 15,000 years ago.
Tug of war was an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920.
Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon in 1969.
The ancient Greek Antikythera mechanism used gears to track the Sun and Moon.
In 1752, Britain and its colonies skipped 11 days to switch calendars.
Ancient Egyptians used a calendar of 365 days.
The Rosetta Stone helped scholars read Egyptian hieroglyphs.
Oxford was teaching students before the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded.
The Lighthouse of Alexandria was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
The oldest zoo still open today was founded in Vienna in 1752.
Ancient Egyptians kept cats as beloved pets thousands of years ago.
The Pony Express carried mail across the American West for only about 18 months.
Africa is the only continent that lies in all four hemispheres.
Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth.
The Sahara is nearly as big as the United States.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert go years without any rain.
Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest when measured from its base on the seafloor.
Alaska has more coastline than all the other US states combined.
Hawaii is the only US state made entirely of islands.
The Grand Canyon is more than a mile deep in places.
Greenland is the largest island in the world.
Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands.
The city of Istanbul sits on two continents, Europe and Asia.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the tallest waterfall on land.
Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world by area.
Brazil is named after a tree called brazilwood.
The Andes are the longest mountain range above water.
The Himalayas formed when India slowly pushed into the rest of Asia.
Chile is about 2,600 miles long but only about 110 miles wide on average.
Venice is built on more than 100 small islands.
About three quarters of Earth's active volcanoes ring the Pacific Ocean.
Counting its overseas lands, France spans more time zones than any other country.
The Caspian Sea is really the largest lake on Earth.
New Zealand has more sheep than people.
The Amazon River carries more water than any other river on Earth.
The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest land on Earth.
Mount Everest's peak is made of rock that was once the floor of an ancient sea.
The Mississippi River starts as a small stream you can walk across in Minnesota.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
The Atlantic Ocean is saltier than the Pacific.
The Sargasso Sea is the only sea without any coastline.
Lemurs are native only to Madagascar.
Rhode Island is the smallest US state by area.
The dot over a lowercase i or j is called a tittle.
The sentence "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" uses every letter.
The word "alphabet" comes from alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters.
The & sign is called an ampersand, and it began as a way to write the Latin "et."
The # sign is sometimes called an octothorpe.
A palindrome reads the same forward and backward, like "racecar."
The word "robot" comes from a Czech play written in 1920.
The word "nerd" first appeared in a Dr. Seuss book in 1950.
The word "bookkeeper" has three double letters in a row.
The Hawaiian alphabet has just 13 letters.
The word "muscle" comes from the Latin for "little mouse."
The sandwich is named after the Earl of Sandwich.
The word "trivia" comes from the Latin for "three roads."
"OK" began in 1839 as a joke spelling of "all correct."
The word "emoji" comes from Japanese and is not related to "emotion."
American Sign Language and British Sign Language are very different languages.
Papua New Guinea is home to more than 800 languages.
A spoonerism swaps sounds, like saying "tease my ears" for "ease my tears."
The word "galaxy" comes from the Greek word for milk.
LEGO comes from the Danish words "leg godt," which mean "play well."
The word "pajamas" comes from Hindi and Persian words for leg clothing.
The word "ketchup" likely comes from a fish sauce from southern China.
The word "jumbo" came to mean huge thanks to a famous elephant named Jumbo.
The word "umbrella" comes from the Latin for "little shadow."
The word "window" comes from Old Norse for "wind eye."
The letter W got its name because it began as two U shapes written side by side.
The word "daisy" comes from "day's eye," because the flower opens at dawn.
A word that means the opposite of itself, like "dust," is called a contronym.
The word "typewriter" can be typed using only the top row of letters.
Honey hardly ever spoils, because it is too sugary and acidic for germs to grow.
Apples, pears, and plums all belong to the rose family.
Popcorn pops because water inside each kernel turns to steam.
The Maya and Aztecs drank chocolate as a bitter, frothy drink.
In 1995, potato plants grew tiny new potatoes aboard the space shuttle Columbia.
White chocolate has cocoa butter but no cocoa solids.
Each cashew nut grows at the bottom of a fruit called a cashew apple.
Avocados don't ripen on the tree, only after they are picked.
Almonds are the seeds of a fruit closely related to peaches.
Broccoli, cabbage, kale, and cauliflower all come from the same wild plant.
Fortune cookies were most likely first made in California, not China.
Most "wasabi" served outside Japan is really horseradish dyed green.
Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit.
Saffron comes from tiny threads inside crocus flowers.
Peaches and nectarines are the same species of fruit.
In warm places, ripe oranges can stay green on the outside.
The holes in Swiss cheese are called eyes.
Chili peppers get their heat from capsaicin, which birds can't taste.
Cacao pods grow right out of the trunk of the cacao tree.
Fresh pineapple has an enzyme that breaks down protein.
A raspberry is made of many tiny fruits called drupelets.
Onions make you cry because cutting them releases a gas that stings your eyes.
Kiwifruit was once called the Chinese gooseberry.
The chocolate chip cookie was invented at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts.
Cheese was likely first made more than 7,000 years ago.
Corn was first grown in Mexico about 9,000 years ago.
Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Count the seconds between lightning and thunder, and five seconds is about a mile.
Diamonds and pencil graphite are both made of pure carbon.
Snowflakes almost always have six sides.
A rainbow is really a full circle, but the ground usually hides the bottom half.
Gold can be hammered into sheets thinner than a human hair.
A puffy white cloud can weigh about a million pounds.
Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats.
Earth's inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Earth bulges a little at the equator, so it isn't a perfect sphere.
Falling raindrops are shaped more like hamburger buns than teardrops.
Fog is a cloud that touches the ground.
Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature.
The metal gallium melts at about 86 degrees Fahrenheit, so it can melt in your hand.
Earth's magnetic north pole slowly wanders across the Arctic.
Light travels about 186,000 miles in one second.
Water boils at a lower temperature on a mountaintop.
Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.
Amber can hold insects trapped inside it for millions of years.
Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.
At the equator, Earth's surface spins at about 1,000 miles an hour.
Hailstones grow in layers, a bit like an onion.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident in 1928.
X-rays were discovered by accident in 1895.
Bubbles are round because a sphere holds air with the least surface.
Water striders walk on water thanks to its springy surface tension.
Lava can be hotter than 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit.
Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
Water is the only common substance found naturally as a solid, liquid, and gas.
Days on Earth were about half an hour shorter in the time of the dinosaurs.
An object weighs less on the Moon, about one sixth of its weight on Earth.
The sky looks blue because air scatters blue sunlight more than red.
A tornado's winds can spin faster than 200 miles an hour.
Hurricanes spin counterclockwise north of the equator, clockwise south of it.
The microwave oven was invented after a radar engineer's candy bar melted.
Bubble wrap was first meant to be textured wallpaper.
The Slinky was invented after a naval engineer saw a spring tumble off a shelf.
Play-Doh started out as a wallpaper cleaner.
Velcro was inspired by burrs that stuck to a dog's fur.
Post-it Notes grew out of a glue that was not sticky enough.
The first computer mouse had a wooden shell.
Crayola crayons first went on sale in 1903.
Thomas Edison's phonograph, made in 1877, could record sound and play it back.
One of the first electric traffic lights went up in Cleveland in 1914.
The Ferris wheel was built for the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago.
The first bicycles had no pedals, so riders pushed off the ground.
Pencil "lead" is really a mix of graphite and clay.
Kites were invented in China more than 2,000 years ago.
The zipper got its name from a brand of rubber boots.
The first webcam watched a coffee pot at Cambridge University.
Eyeglasses were invented in Italy around 1290.
Earmuffs were patented by a teenager from Maine.
Louis Braille created his reading system for the blind as a teenager.
The first product scanned by a barcode in a store was a pack of gum.
The Frisbee was named after a bakery whose pie tins people tossed for fun.
The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago.
Mary Anderson patented the windshield wiper in 1903.
Josephine Cochrane patented a working dishwasher in 1886.
Jigsaw puzzles were first made to help children learn maps.
Fireworks were invented in China more than 1,000 years ago.
Bubble gum was invented in 1928 and colored pink because that dye was handy.
One of the first roller coasters built just for fun opened at Coney Island in 1884.
The ice cream scoop with a release lever was patented by Alfred Cralle in 1897.
The first car with a gas engine was built by Karl Benz in 1885.
The digits of pi go on forever without settling into a repeating pattern.
A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros.
Multiply any whole number by 9, and its digits add up to a multiple of 9.
In a group of just 23 people, there is about a 50 percent chance two share a birthday.
A well shuffled deck of cards is almost surely in an order never seen before.
Bees build hexagons because they hold the most honey for the least wax.
Every odd number has the letter "e" in its English name.
Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde invented the equals sign in 1557.
Pinecones and sunflowers grow in spirals that follow Fibonacci numbers.
There are infinitely many prime numbers, as Euclid proved long ago.
The number 1 is not a prime number.
A Mobius strip has only one side and one edge.
A dozen dozen, or 144, is called a gross.
Minus 40 degrees is the same in Fahrenheit and Celsius.
There are exactly five Platonic solids, and a cube is one of them.
Ancient Babylonians counted in 60s, and that's why an hour has 60 minutes.
In Old English, the word "hundred" could mean 120.
The infinity symbol is called a lemniscate.
A leap year skips century years, unless they divide evenly by 400.
A tesseract is a cube stretched into a fourth dimension.
In a magic square, every row, column, and diagonal adds up to the same number.
The number 6 is perfect, because 1 plus 2 plus 3 equals 6.
A circle has the most area of any shape with the same perimeter.
The word "geometry" means "earth measuring" in Greek.
Our digits 0 to 9 came from India and spread through the Arab world.
Any map can be colored with just four colors so no neighbors match.
Computers store everything using just two digits, 0 and 1.
The ancient Egyptians used fractions, but almost always with a 1 on top.
A soccer ball pattern uses 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
If you fold a paper in half 7 times, it gets 128 layers thick.
